newsitem.title: ALGERIA: Algeria count nears end, opposition cries foul.
newsitem.headline: Algeria count nears end, opposition cries foul.

text.p: Algerian officials neared the end of counting on Friday in the vast North African country's first parliamentary election for five violence-filled years.
The interior minister promised results during Friday on the poll which the authorities hope will start to bring the country out of crisis which they blame on Moslem fundamentalists.
A pro-government party forecast it was doing well, while two opposition parties cried foul.

"We are in a very respectable position," National Democratic Rally (RND) spokesman Hamraoui Habib Chawki told Reuters. "The results that we have from the various provinces put the party constantly in the top three positions."
But Chawki hinted that the party would not be able to gain an absolute majority at the 380-seat National Assembly, the lower house.
"From now on there will not be any single dominant force. This will help the development of democracy and diversify the lower house," he said.

The Islam-orientated Movement of a Peaceful Society (MPS) and the secular Socialist Forces Front (FFS) alleged irregularities in the ballot in which around 10 million people, 66.3 percent of the electorate, cast their votes.

The election was the first since Moslem fundamentalists dominated a December 1991 poll. The military-backed authorities cancelled that election in January 1992 and shortly afterwards the country plunged into violence in which an estimated 60,000 people died.

President Liamine Zeroual sees the poll as a key towards ending the crisis in the oil and gas producing country and the authorities depoyed about 200,000 security forces to guard the 16.7 million voters.
In one of only two reports of violence, MPS leader Mahfoud Nahnah said: "A real massacre took place in which there were (people) killed and wounded in Boudgham district."
He said the killing, in the western town of Tlemcen was "related to the elections", but refused to give any other detail. There was no official comment on the report or other confirmation.
The other report of violence also came from MPS sources who said earlier that two local poll observers had been wounded in a bomb blast in their car near the central town of Djelfa.
Interior Minister Mustapha Benmansour promised full results after 11 a.m. (1000 GMT) on Friday and also dismissed charges of irregularities in the poll being monitored by international observers.
A new proportional representation law makes it very difficult for a single party to gain an absolute majority. More than 7,000 candidates stood in the ballot representing 39 political parties.
The U.S. State Department praised the voters for turning out in force saying they had shown "courage because they have been subjected to the most vicious case of terrorism over many, many years".
A wave of bombings in Algiers by suspected Moslem rebels killed 22 people and wounded more than 120 in Algiers just days before the runup to the election.
The 43.27 percent turnout in capital, where 24 seats are at stake, was the lowest in the country, according to the Interior Ministry.
"I voted for peace," Ahmed Yanaguen, 58, said after he and his wife, wearing a black veil, were the first to vote at El-Warda school in the capital's Telemly neighbourhood.

Sceptics in the Algerian capital doubt the level of violence would soon drop because the new assembly will be deprived of any real power, which rests with the president, and will not be able to push for dialogue with radical Islamists.
